To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
South Africa's health sector has a machine bureaucracy structure and culture that limits the success of administrative reforms to integrate disease programmes.
the health system is configured as Mintzberg’s machine bureaucracy, with structures, management and practices that undermine the administrative integration of HIV services in districts.

the health system in South Africa can be characterized as a machine bureaucracy, which is centralized and highly rules-based with structures and practices that promote HIV programme managers as lead players in monitoring HIV interventions in districts, and that this undermines policy objectives of promoting district managers as leaders of HIV monitoring in the districts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of why administrative integration has not been achieved in the health sector in South Africa and what can be done about it.
the organizational and managerial conditions that may support or hinder the integration of health services.
the organizational and cultural factors that may be limiting the achievement of the administrative integration of DCPs within South Africa's health sector.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the organizational culture and structure of the health system in South Africa is configured to support a centralized, formalized and rules based model of HIV service monitoring and evaluation.
the health system configuration is a machine bureaucracy.
the health system is not configured to support administrative health service integration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the health system is configured as a machine bureaucracy, with a highly formalized and centralized system, with structures, practices, and management styles that undermine the policy objective of district managers assuming the leadership role.
health systems are complex adaptive systems that are not easily changed by policy interventions.
administrative integration reforms require a more decentralized and less formalized health system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
administrative integration reforms are unlikely to succeed if the organizational structures, culture and practices that underpin them are not aligned.
health sector reforms need to consider the influence of organizational culture, structures and practices, and how these may be modified to support integration.
the health system is not designed to support administrative integration, and that the design of HIV M&E systems is a useful lens through which to understand this.
